title: Quantum models of interaction Hamiltonian and their paradoxes
authors: Nicolas Gisin, Serge Massar, Jef Pauwels, Pavel Sekatski
abstract: In quantum physics it is commonplace to model the interaction of remote systems with a many-body Hamiltonian. Taking such an action-at-a-distance description {\it à la lettre} leads to various paradoxes related to faster-than-light communication and apparent inconsistencies in local energy accounting. It also neglects residual effects, such as entanglement between the remote systems and the mediator that implements the interaction, or the decoherence that arises when the remote systems undergo local evolution. We study simple microscopic quantum models that respect the light cone by design and reproduce two-body Hamiltonians. For these models we quantitatively analyze the residual effects of the microscopic mediator on the remote systems, including dressing of stationary states, and decoherence in the presence of fast local control. We show how the models resolve the paradoxes.
summary: This theoretical paper investigates the inconsistencies arising from treating quantum interactions as instantaneous, nonlocal Hamiltonians. It resolves these paradoxes by modeling the interaction through a physical mediator field that respects the speed of light. The methodology involves time-averaging and perturbation theory to show how residual mediator effects cause decoherence and correct the effective dynamics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the paradoxes arising when modeling interactions between remote quantum systems using an effective, nonlocal Hamiltonian that violates fundamental principles like locality and finite propagation speed.
main_result: The paradoxes are resolved by embedding the interaction into a microscopic mediator model that explicitly respects the light cone and finite mediator flight time, leading to measurable residual effects and decoherence.
method: The analysis employs time-averaging (coarse-graining) over the mediator flight time and utilizes perturbative expansions in the coupling strength to derive effective Hamiltonians and master equations.
model_or_system: The system consists of two remote quantum systems (A and B) coupled via a microscopic mediator (M), which can be modeled as a bosonic field in a waveguide or through successive local unitary transformations.
key_observables: Faster-than-light communication signatures, local energy cost/work, purity ($	ext{Tr}( ar{ho}(t)^2)$), and decoherence rates.
important_parameters: Mediator flight time ($T$), local coupling strength ($g$), and the effective coupling constant ($\mu$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on deriving effective descriptions by tracing out the mediator field, assuming the mediator respects causality (light cone), and using approximations like the continuum limit.
figures_summary: Not specified by the notes, but the analysis involves deriving time-averaged density matrices and examining state evolution under local gates.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the paradoxes of nonlocal Hamiltonians to constructing microscopic, causal mediator models. It then analyzes the resulting dynamics using time averaging and perturbative expansions, culminating in discussions of decoherence and state-dependent evolution.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum optics as it provides a rigorous framework for deriving effective Hamiltonians from underlying local, causal interactions mediated by quantum fields, addressing fundamental issues of locality and information transfer.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Space-time diagram of a mediator interacting with systems A and B, giving rise to an interaction eig2AB ⊗1M. Systems A and B are separated by distance L. The mediator travels at speed v, hence takes time T = L/v to go from one system to the other. While the mediator trajectory is well defined in space-time, the effective interaction arises after the mediator has finished all its interactions and cannot be localized exactly in space-time.

FIG. 2. Space-time diagrams of mediators (in black) contin- uously interacting with systems A (red) and B (blue). The interactions of the mediators with the A and B systems are shown by black dots. The mediators take time T to travel from A to B (or back). A new mediator arrives every τ. In panel (a) τ = 4T while in panel (b) τ ≪T. In the limit τ →0 we obtain the continuous field model. Both models give rise to an effective interaction Hamiltonian Heff AB.

FIG. 3. Spatial arrangement of systems A (red) and B (blue) and the mediators (stars), used to illustrate dressed states. The mediators arrive at a rate 1/τ = 1/T, ensuring that the mediator configuration repeats every T.

FIG. 4. Spatial arrangement of systems A (red) and B (blue) and the mediator modes (stars). There are n modes between A and B. In one elementary time step the modes hop forward by one position, and those at positions 0, n, 2n, and 3n interact with A or B.

FIG. 5. Local control resolves the mediator dynamics. (a) In a discrete loop, arbitrary evolution of Alice’s coupling observable between the two encounters is captured by the mismatch ∆A = At+2T −At; sudden gates and slowly varying control are two limits of the same expression. (b) For a continuous mediator flux, an instantaneous gate is exactly tractable and emits a disturbed pulse of duration 2T. (c) The most general setting combines a continuous mediator field with continuous local control hA(t). In this case, a continuous flux of disturbed mediators is emitted. Its detailed analysis is left open.
